During a change of state the temperature stays constant although heat is supplied: the curve is flat, at the melting point for melting and at the boiling point for boiling.

There are two flat parts. The lower one, B to C at $0\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, is the melting. The upper one, D to E at $100\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, is the boiling.

questions.enonce_markdown: An object is placed $30\ \text{cm}$ from a converging lens of focal length $10\ \text{cm}$. The image distance is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
For a lens, $\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{u}+\dfrac{1}{v}$, where $u$ is the object distance and $v$ the image distance.

$\dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{3-1}{30}=\dfrac{2}{30}$, so $v=15\ \text{cm}$.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
Subtract the reciprocals before inverting: do not subtract $f-u$ directly.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Refraction and lenses: refractive index, critical angle and the lens formula
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: For a lens, $\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{u}+\dfrac{1}{v}$, where $u$ is the object distance and $v$ the image distance.

questions.enonce_markdown: A wave of frequency $25\ \text{Hz}$ has a wavelength of $12\ \text{m}$. The speed of the wave is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The wave equation is $v=f\lambda$: speed is frequency multiplied by wavelength.

$v=25\times12=300\ \text{m/s}$.

**Answer: D.**

rappels_de_methode.competence: Waves: properties, wave types and the wave equation
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: The wave equation is $v=f\lambda$: speed is frequency multiplied by wavelength.

Conduction and convection need particles of matter to carry the heat, while radiation travels as electromagnetic waves.

The heat of the Sun reaches the Earth through the vacuum of space by radiation.

**Answer: D.**

The pressure due to a liquid column is $P=h\rho g$, where $h$ is the depth.

$P=15\times1\,000\times10=150\,000=1.5\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A pump raises $200\ \text{kg}$ of water through a height of $6\ \text{m}$ in $20\ \text{s}$. Taking $g=10\ \text{m/s}^{2}$, the power of the pump is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Power is the work done divided by the time taken, and the work done in lifting is $mgh$.

Work: $200\times10\times6=12\,000\ \text{J}$. Power: $\dfrac{12\,000}{20}=600\ \text{W}$.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
$12\,000$ is the work in joules: it must still be divided by the time.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Work, energy and power: calculations, efficiency and energy sources
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Power is the work done divided by the time taken, and the work done in lifting is $mgh$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A ray of light enters glass at an angle of incidence of $45^{\circ}$ and is refracted at an angle of $30^{\circ}$. The refractive index of the glass is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Snell's law: the refractive index is $n=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$, using the sines of the angles.

$n=\dfrac{\sin45^{\circ}}{\sin30^{\circ}}=\dfrac{0.707}{0.5}=1.41\approx1.4$.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
Use the sines, not the angles: $\dfrac{45}{30}=1.5$ is wrong, and $0.7$ comes from inverting the ratio.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Refraction of light
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Snell's law: the refractive index is $n=\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$, using the sines of the angles.

Each part of the electromagnetic spectrum has its uses: radio waves for broadcasting, infrared for heating and remote controls, X-rays for medical images.

questions.enonce_markdown: The specific heat capacity of water is $4\,200\ \text{J/kg K}$. The heat needed to raise the temperature of $2\ \text{kg}$ of water from $20\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $70\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The heat needed to change the temperature of a body is $Q=mc\Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta$ is the change in temperature.

$\Delta\theta=70-20=50\ \text{K}$, so $Q=2\times4\,200\times50=420\,000\ \text{J}$.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
Use the temperature change, $50\ \text{K}$, not the final temperature $70\,^{\circ}\text{C}$.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Thermal physics: heat, specific heat capacity and changes of state
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: The heat needed to change the temperature of a body is $Q=mc\Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta$ is the change in temperature.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main scale of a micrometer screw gauge reads $2.5\ \text{mm}$ and the thimble reads $34$ divisions, each division being $0.01\ \text{mm}$. The diameter of the wire is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
A micrometer reading is the main scale reading plus the thimble reading, where the thimble reading is the number of divisions multiplied by $0.01\ \text{mm}$.

Thimble reading: $34\times0.01=0.34\ \text{mm}$. Diameter: $2.5+0.34=2.84\ \text{mm}$.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
$34$ divisions of $0.01\ \text{mm}$ make $0.34\ \text{mm}$, not $0.034\ \text{mm}$.

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: A micrometer reading is the main scale reading plus the thimble reading, where the thimble reading is the number of divisions multiplied by $0.01\ \text{mm}$.

The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic (proton) number: $N=A-Z$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A body of mass $4\ \text{kg}$ moves at a speed of $5\ \text{m/s}$. Its kinetic energy is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Kinetic energy is $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$: the speed is squared, and there is a factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

$\text{KE}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times5^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times25=50\ \text{J}$.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
Leaving out the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $100\ \text{J}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A block has a mass of $540\ \text{g}$ and a volume of $200\ \text{cm}^{3}$. Its density is
questions.corrige_markdown:

Density is mass divided by volume: $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$.

$\rho=\dfrac{540}{200}=2.7\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$.

**Answer: A.**

$0.37\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$ comes from dividing the volume by the mass, the inverse of the density.

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Density is mass divided by volume: $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A pupil times $20$ complete oscillations of a simple pendulum and finds that they take $36\ \text{s}$. The period of the pendulum is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
The period is the time for one complete oscillation: the total time divided by the number of oscillations.

$T=\dfrac{36}{20}=1.8\ \text{s}$. Timing many oscillations gives a more accurate period than timing one.

**Answer: D.**

### Piège à éviter
$0.56\ \text{s}$ is the frequency in hertz, not the period.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Practical physics: measuring, reducing errors and handling results

Follow the energy from its source: water stored high up has gravitational potential energy, flowing water has kinetic energy, and the generator produces electrical energy.

questions.corrige_markdown:

Hooke's law: within the elastic limit the extension is directly proportional to the load.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A trolley of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ moving at $3\ \text{m/s}$ collides with a stationary trolley of mass $1\ \text{kg}$ and the two stick together. Their common velocity is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
In a collision with no external force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

Momentum before: $2\times3+1\times0=6\ \text{kg m/s}$. After the collision the total mass is $3\ \text{kg}$, so $3v=6$ and $v=2\ \text{m/s}$.

**Answer: D.**

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: In a collision with no external force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

questions.corrige_markdown:

Pressure is force divided by the area on which it acts: $P=\dfrac{F}{A}$.

$P=\dfrac{600}{0.03}=20\,000\ \text{Pa}$.

**Answer: C.**

$18\ \text{Pa}$ comes from multiplying the force by the area.

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Pressure is force divided by the area on which it acts: $P=\dfrac{F}{A}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A transformer has $200$ turns on its primary coil and $50$ turns on its secondary coil. The primary coil is connected to a $240\ \text{V}$ a.c. supply. The voltage across the secondary coil is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
For a transformer, $\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}=\dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$: the voltage is in the same ratio as the number of turns.

$V_{s}=240\times\dfrac{50}{200}=60\ \text{V}$. It is a step-down transformer.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
$960\ \text{V}$ comes from inverting the ratio of turns.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Transformers: turns ratio, efficiency and power transmission
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: For a transformer, $\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}=\dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$: the voltage is in the same ratio as the number of turns.

Fleming's left-hand rule is for the motor effect (force on a conductor), and the right-hand rule is for the generator effect (induced current).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A machine with a velocity ratio of $5$ needs an effort of $50\ \text{N}$ to raise a load of $200\ \text{N}$. Its efficiency is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{mechanical advantage}}{\text{velocity ratio}}\times100\%$, and mechanical advantage $=\dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$.

Mechanical advantage: $\dfrac{200}{50}=4$. Efficiency: $\dfrac{4}{5}\times100=80\%$.

**Answer: A.**

### Piège à éviter
An efficiency can never exceed $100\%$: $125\%$ comes from inverting the ratio.

rappels_de_methode.competence: Simple machines: levers, ramps and efficiency
rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{mechanical advantage}}{\text{velocity ratio}}\times100\%$, and mechanical advantage $=\dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A resultant force of $30\ \text{N}$ acts on a trolley of mass $6\ \text{kg}$. The acceleration of the trolley is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Newton's second law: resultant force $=$ mass $\times$ acceleration, so $a=\dfrac{F}{m}$.

$a=\dfrac{30}{6}=5\ \text{m/s}^{2}$.

**Answer: B.**

### Piège à éviter
$0.2\ \text{m/s}^{2}$ is the mass divided by the force.

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Newton's second law: resultant force $=$ mass $\times$ acceleration, so $a=\dfrac{F}{m}$.

questions.corrige_markdown:

The energy needed to change the state of a mass $m$ at constant temperature is $Q=ml$.

**Answer: A.**

$672\,000\ \text{J}$ comes from dividing by the mass, $\dfrac{336\,000}{0.5}$.

questions.enonce_markdown: The gravitational field strength on the Moon is $1.6\ \text{N/kg}$. The weight of a $12\ \text{kg}$ body on the Moon is
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
Weight is mass multiplied by the gravitational field strength: $W=mg$.

$W=12\times1.6=19.2\ \text{N}$. The mass stays $12\ \text{kg}$ everywhere, but the weight depends on $g$.

**Answer: C.**

### Piège à éviter
$120\ \text{N}$ would be the weight on Earth, where $g=10\ \text{N/kg}$.

rappels_de_methode.contenu_markdown: Weight is mass multiplied by the gravitational field strength: $W=mg$.
